chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
title: Hearing Duke Ellington's Jungle Band in Cincinnati
summary: Passing through from the Check and Double Check film, Ellington's small-sectioned band played all original tunes; Jackson lists the men and discusses the jungle sound.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: The only other band that I heard that impressed me was that same year when I was with Zack White. I heard Duke Ellington's band. They came to Cincinnati and they was on the way from California -- they had just made the picture 'Check and Doublecheck' with Amos and Andy -- and they only had five brass at that time and just three saxophones. The brass was Whetsol, Metzel and Cootie Williams and Freddie Jenkins. That was the trumpets.
Yeah, and only two trombones, just Tizol and Tricky Sam, Joe Norton.
Only two. And the saxophones was Johnny Hodges and Harry Carney and --
And at that time, you know, Harry was playing some first, too. He was playing some lead alto.
Sure. There is no record of Rockin' I'll and Rhythm. Harry's playing lead alto on that.
And, you know, he's one of the co-writers, too, of Rockin' and Rhythm.
Yeah. And, of course, William Brode was the bass player.
-- and Freddy Guy. And you couldn't get close to the bandstand. And I listened to that band and I said, "What are they playing?" Because they wasn't playing none of the tunes that we knew.
It was all original tunes of Duke, and they called it the Jungle Band in those days, you know.
Right. I guess they did that to make it a black band like they did McKinney's Cottonpickers, and they called it the Cottonpickers to make it identified with black.
I don't think so much that as it was that the type of music they played was jungle music.
Uh-huh, tom-toms, a lot of tom-toms.
Exactly. A lot of tom-toms and growling and sounds.
Even like sounds in the jungle, you know.
Fantastic that, you know, the mind this man had.
